text: Every Azure VM's storage is backed by a Managed Disk — Microsoft handles the underlying storage account for you entirely, so you just pick a size and a performance tier instead of worrying about the storage-account IOPS limits administrators used to manage under the older unmanaged-disk model, where too many disks crammed into one account could hit a shared ceiling.

Each VM gets exactly one OS disk, holding the operating system, and can have zero or more data disks attached for application data, databases, or logs. Keeping application data on its own data disk rather than the OS disk is standard practice, since a data disk can be resized, snapshotted, or moved independently of the operating system underneath it.

Managed Disks come in four tiers, each a real tradeoff between cost, IOPS, and latency. Standard HDD is spinning-disk-backed and cheapest, with higher and less consistent latency, fitting backups, archival data, and dev/test. Standard SSD is SSD-backed with steadier latency and still budget-friendly, fitting web servers and light production load. Premium SSD delivers high IOPS and low, consistent latency for production databases and I/O-intensive workloads. Ultra Disk sits on top of all three, letting you adjust IOPS and throughput independently on the fly without detaching the disk, for the most demanding workloads like large transactional databases.

Creating a disk and attaching it to a VM is two commands: az disk create with a resource group, a size in GB, and a sku like Premium_LRS, then az vm disk attach pointing that disk at the VM by name. Premium and Ultra tiers specifically require a VM size that supports premium storage — sizes with an s in the name, like Standard_D2s_v5, rather than a plain Standard_D2_v5.

Pick the tier the workload actually needs, not the most expensive one by default: Standard HDD for rarely-touched data, Standard SSD for general production storage that isn't performance-critical, and Premium SSD or Ultra Disk specifically when latency spikes would genuinely hurt the application. Next: Virtual Machine Scale Sets, where identical VMs run behind autoscale rules to absorb variable load automatically.
